stem: A marketing manager rewrites customer emails in the company's brand voice several times a week. Each time she opens a new chat and pastes the same three-page style guide before asking for help. Which Claude feature removes this repetition?

options.text: A Project with the style guide added as knowledge and the voice rules written as the Project's instructions.
options.why: Project knowledge and instructions persist across every chat in the Project, so the style guide is available without pasting it again.

options.text: Research mode, so Claude can look up the brand voice each time.
options.why: Research gathers information from the web and connected sources; it does not store a document for reuse across chats.

options.text: An artifact containing the style guide, opened in each new chat.
options.why: An artifact is an output Claude creates within a conversation; it is not a mechanism for supplying context to future chats.

options.text: Keeping a single chat open indefinitely for all brand-voice rewrites, so the style guide pasted at the start remains in the conversation.
options.why: One ever-growing chat eventually degrades and reaches the length limit, and it mixes dozens of unrelated emails into one thread.

explanation: Projects are self-contained workspaces whose knowledge and custom instructions persist across all chats inside them. Recurring context such as a style guide belongs in a Project, not in every prompt.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects

stem: An operations analyst has been asked for a comparison of five SaaS tools, including their current pricing tiers, recent customer reviews and any acquisitions in the past year, with citations for every claim. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Turn on Research and ask for the comparison, requesting sources and retrieval dates for each claim.
options.why: Research runs multiple searches that build on each other across the web and connected sources and returns a report with easy-to-check citations, which is what a sourced multi-step comparison needs.

options.text: Create a Project named after the comparison and ask the question inside it.
options.why: A Project stores context and instructions; on its own it does not fetch current information from the web.

options.text: Ask in a plain chat with web search off, relying on what Claude already knows about the five tools and asking it to mark any claim it is not sure about.
options.why: Training knowledge is not current and carries no citations; pricing tiers and recent acquisitions change too often to answer from memory.

options.text: Ask Claude to build the comparison as an artifact table first, then verify each cell manually.
options.why: An artifact is the right container for the finished table, but it does not gather current, sourced information; the research step still has to happen.

explanation: Research is designed for comprehensive information gathering that needs several searches and synthesis across sources, with citations. Plain chat from training knowledge, a Project, or an artifact alone does not provide current, sourced facts.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use research on Claude; When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?

stem: A team lead is deciding which of her requests should be produced as artifacts rather than as inline chat replies. Which two are best suited to artifacts? (Choose two.)

options.text: A one-page new-starter checklist that she will edit, version and share with three other managers.
options.why: A substantial, self-contained document that will be edited, iterated and reused is exactly what artifacts are for.

options.text: A quick question about whether a public holiday falls on a Monday this year.
options.why: A one-line factual answer belongs inline; an artifact would add overhead for no reuse benefit.

options.text: A departmental budget table she wants to refine over several rounds and paste into a report.
options.why: A structured table that will be revised repeatedly and lifted out of the conversation benefits from the artifact's editing and versioning.

options.text: Storing the department's style guide so that future chats can use it.
options.why: Persisting context for future chats is a Project's job; artifacts are outputs of a conversation, not a knowledge store.

options.text: Finding the latest changes to a regulation her team must follow.
options.why: Current, sourced information calls for web search or Research; an artifact only presents content, it does not gather it.

explanation: Claude creates artifacts for significant, self-contained content that you are likely to edit, iterate on or reuse outside the conversation: documents, tables, code, diagrams and small tools. Short answers stay inline; stored context goes in a Project; current facts come from search or Research.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are artifacts and how do I use them

stem: A consulting partner wants a simple interactive scenario calculator for a client, built from the assumptions in a 20-page engagement brief. Two consultants will refine it over three weeks in separate sessions, and every version must respect the brief's assumptions. Which combination of features fits best?

options.text: A plain chat each time, pasting the brief and the previous version of the calculator at the start of every session.
options.why: Re-pasting a 20-page brief in every session is error-prone, and each new chat has no link to the previous version unless it is pasted too.

options.text: A Project holding the brief as knowledge with the key assumptions in its instructions, with the calculator built and iterated as an artifact in chats inside that Project.
options.why: The Project keeps the brief and assumptions in front of both consultants across sessions, and the artifact gives the calculator a persistent, editable, versioned form.

options.text: Research mode, so Claude can look up scenario-calculator best practices and generate the tool from them.
options.why: Research gathers external information; the calculator's inputs are the client's own brief, which does not need web research and would not be persisted by it.

options.text: Turning on memory so Claude remembers the brief, then building the calculator in ordinary chats.
options.why: Memory captures preferences and working context, not a 20-page document with specific figures; it is not a reliable store for the brief's assumptions.

explanation: Recurring, shared context belongs in a Project; a deliverable that is edited and versioned belongs in an artifact. Combining them gives both consultants the same assumptions and the same evolving tool across sessions. Research and memory solve different problems.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects; What are artifacts and how do I use them

stem: An HR operations lead runs a monthly task: check the latest employment-law updates in three countries, compare them against the internal policy handbook, and produce a change summary for legal review. The handbook is 90 pages and changes twice a year; the comparison rules are the same every month. Which setup satisfies the recurring nature, the need for current external information and the need to compare against the handbook?

options.text: Each month, open a plain chat, paste the handbook, turn on Research, and ask for the comparison.
options.why: It works once, but pasting 90 pages and retyping the comparison rules every month is wasteful and drifts; the recurring parts are not persisted.

options.text: Keep one chat open all year and add each month's request to it so Claude can see the previous comparisons.
options.why: A year-long chat grows past the length limit and degrades; earlier months' searches also clutter the context for the current comparison.

options.text: Create a Project with the handbook as knowledge and the comparison rules as instructions, run Research inside a new chat in that Project each month, and produce the summary as an artifact for legal.
options.why: The Project persists the handbook and rules, Research supplies the current legal updates and their sources, and the artifact gives legal a clean, editable deliverable.

options.text: Turn on memory so Claude retains the handbook, and rely on its training knowledge for the legal updates.
options.why: Memory is not a document store for a 90-page handbook, and training knowledge cannot supply this month's legal changes with sources.

explanation: Match each need to the feature built for it: Projects for recurring context and rules, Research for sourced multi-step external information, artifacts for the deliverable. Running Research inside a Project combines persistent internal context with current external facts.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects; Use research on Claude; What are artifacts and how do I use them

stem: A new team member asks how the Claude models in the model picker differ from each other. Which description is correct?

options.text: Haiku is the most capable model for hard reasoning; Opus is the fastest and lightest option for quick lookups.
options.why: This reverses the tiers: Haiku is the fast, lightweight model and Opus is the most capable for complex reasoning.

options.text: Sonnet is intended only for writing code; Haiku and Opus are for all other business tasks.
options.why: Sonnet is the balanced everyday model for writing, analysis, questions and coding alike; no tier is limited to code.

options.text: All three tiers produce the same quality; the only difference is which one is selected by default.
options.why: The tiers trade off speed and efficiency against reasoning depth; that trade-off is the whole reason to choose between them.

options.text: Haiku is the fastest, lightest tier for simple high-volume work; Sonnet is the balanced default for most tasks; Opus is the most capable tier for the hardest reasoning.
options.why: This matches how the help centre characterises the picker: Haiku for speed, Sonnet as the everyday workhorse, Opus for maximum reasoning power.

explanation: The three tiers form a speed-versus-depth ladder. Haiku is fastest and suited to quick, simple, high-volume tasks; Sonnet balances speed and capability for the vast majority of work; Opus is reserved for genuinely complex, multi-step problems where quality matters more than speed.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: A project coordinator needs to sort 2,000 short support tickets into six fixed categories using a simple, well-defined rule set. The work is repetitive, each ticket is two or three sentences, and results are needed by the end of the day. Which model tier fits?

options.text: Opus, because the largest volume of items deserves the most capable model.
options.why: Volume is not complexity; using the slowest, most resource-intensive tier on 2,000 trivial classifications wastes time and usage.

options.text: Haiku, because the task is simple, rule-based and high-volume, so speed and efficiency matter more than deep reasoning.
options.why: Short, straightforward, repetitive classification is the textbook fit for the fastest, lightest tier.

options.text: Sonnet with extended thinking turned on, so each ticket is reasoned about carefully and borderline cases between the six categories are handled well.
options.why: Extended thinking adds time per ticket for a task that needs no deliberation; it works against the end-of-day deadline.

options.text: Alternate between Opus and Haiku ticket by ticket to average out quality and speed.
options.why: Alternating tiers gives inconsistent handling of identical tasks and no benefit; the task calls for one appropriate tier.

explanation: Haiku suits quick lookups, simple edits and high-volume, straightforward tasks where speed and efficiency matter more than reasoning depth. Reserve heavier tiers and extended thinking for problems that need them.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: An education director is preparing a five-year curriculum strategy that must reconcile accreditation requirements, a shrinking budget and a phased hiring plan. She will run the analysis once and quality matters far more than turnaround time. Which model tier fits?

options.text: Opus, because this is a genuinely complex multi-constraint problem where reasoning quality matters more than speed.
options.why: The most capable tier is intended for the hardest, multi-step reasoning tasks where a slower, more thorough answer is worth it, which describes a one-off strategic analysis.

options.text: Whichever model was used in her last conversation, since the picker remembers it.
options.why: The picker's default is a convenience, not a recommendation; the tier should be chosen for the task's demands.

options.text: Haiku, so the strategy is produced as quickly as possible.
options.why: Speed is not the priority here, and the lightest tier is the least suited to weighing several interacting constraints over a multi-year horizon.

options.text: Sonnet, because it is the balanced default designed for the vast majority of tasks and should be used unless it has already failed on the specific task.
options.why: Sonnet is the right default for everyday work, but the help centre reserves Opus for genuinely complex, multi-step problems where quality outweighs speed, which is the case here.

explanation: Opus is for the hardest work: complex, multi-step problems with interacting constraints, run when quality matters more than speed or volume. A one-off strategic analysis with several trade-offs is that case; the default tier remains right for routine tasks.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: A communications manager is writing a one-page internal guide on choosing between Claude models. Which three statements are accurate enough to include? (Choose three.)

options.text: Switching models part-way through a conversation keeps the conversation history; the new model sees what the previous one produced.
options.why: The help centre confirms that changing the model does not clear the conversation and that the change applies from the next response.

options.text: Opus never produces incorrect facts, so outputs from it do not need checking.
options.why: Every tier can produce plausible but wrong details; a more capable model reduces error rates but does not remove the need for verification.

options.text: Haiku trades some reasoning depth for speed and efficiency, which makes it the right choice for simple, high-volume tasks.
options.why: This is the defining trade-off of the lightest tier and the reason it exists alongside the others.

options.text: Haiku cannot follow structured instructions or return tables, so any formatted output needs Sonnet or Opus.
options.why: Haiku follows instructions and produces structured output; its limitation is depth of reasoning on hard problems, not formatting.

options.text: Sonnet is the balanced everyday choice for most writing, analysis and question-answering tasks.
options.why: The help centre describes Sonnet as the daily driver designed for the vast majority of tasks.

options.text: Choosing a larger model lets Claude remember earlier conversations that smaller models forget.
options.why: Cross-conversation memory comes from the memory feature, Projects or chat search, not from the model tier.

explanation: Accurate guidance on model types covers the speed-versus-depth trade-off (Haiku fast and light, Sonnet balanced, Opus most capable) and the mechanics of switching, which preserves history. It should not claim any tier is infallible, that Haiku cannot format, or that model size governs memory.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings; Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context

stem: After one poor Haiku result on a complex crisis-communications analysis, a communications team standardised on Opus for everything. Three months later they report hitting usage limits by mid-afternoon and slow turnaround on the roughly 300 short headline and subject-line rewrites they do each day, while still needing occasional deep analyses. Which model policy resolves all of these?

options.text: Stay on Opus for everything and request a higher usage allowance so the limits stop interrupting the day.
options.why: More allowance does not fix the slow turnaround on hundreds of trivial rewrites, and it entrenches the mismatch between task and tier.

options.text: Switch everything to Haiku, since the volume of simple work dwarfs the occasional analysis.
options.why: The original Haiku failure was on exactly the kind of complex analysis the team still needs; using the lightest tier everywhere repeats that mistake.

options.text: Use Haiku for the daily high-volume rewrites, Sonnet as the default for ordinary drafting and analysis, and reserve Opus for the genuinely complex analyses.
options.why: Matching each class of task to its tier restores speed and usage headroom on the simple work while keeping the most capable model for the problems that need it.

options.text: Use Sonnet for everything, since it balances speed and capability, avoids the need for staff to choose a model per task, and has not been the source of any complaint so far.
options.why: A single balanced tier is defensible, but it still spends more than needed on 300 trivial rewrites a day and gives up the top tier on the crisis analyses the team explicitly still needs.

explanation: One bad result on one task is not a reason to move all work to the heaviest tier. Sort the workload by difficulty and volume: the fastest model for simple high-volume tasks, the balanced model as default, and the most capable model only where reasoning depth is decisive.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings; Usage limit best practices

stem: A communications assistant must produce one-sentence summaries of about 500 news items every morning before 8 a.m. The summaries are simple and low-stakes, and the deadline is tight. Which choice best aligns the model with the task requirements?

options.text: The most capable tier for every item, to guarantee the best possible sentence each time, since the summaries are read by senior leaders first thing in the morning.
options.why: Maximum reasoning power is wasted on a one-sentence summary and makes 500 items slower and more usage-intensive than the deadline allows.

options.text: No model at all: skip the summaries because 500 items is too many.
options.why: The volume is exactly what a fast model handles well; abandoning the task ignores an appropriate fit that exists.

options.text: The most capable tier with extended thinking, so each summary is deliberated over.
options.why: Deliberation adds time per item to a task that needs none; it works directly against the 8 a.m. deadline.

options.text: The fastest, lightest tier, because the task is simple and high-volume and speed matters more than depth.
options.why: Aligning model selection with the task means matching a fast, efficient model to straightforward, high-volume work.

explanation: Model fit means weighing speed, cost and quality against what the task actually needs. Simple, high-volume, time-boxed work is the clearest case for the fastest tier; reserve deeper tiers for tasks where reasoning quality changes the outcome.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: A consultant has one week to synthesise an 80-page due-diligence pack into a recommendation that a client will use to decide on a major acquisition. It is a one-off task, an error would be very costly, and there is no time pressure within the week. Which model choice fits these requirements?

options.text: The fastest tier, so several drafts can be produced and the best one selected.
options.why: Producing many quick drafts does not substitute for reasoning depth on a high-stakes, multi-constraint synthesis; speed is not what this task rewards.

options.text: The balanced tier, because it is the recommended default for most work and the most capable tier should only be tried if the balanced tier's output proves inadequate.
options.why: Waiting for a failure on a decision this costly is the wrong order; the stakes and complexity justify the most capable tier from the start.

options.text: The fastest tier with a higher effort setting, to combine speed with quality.
options.why: Effort and thinking settings tune how much work a model does, but they do not turn the lightest tier into the best reasoner for the hardest tasks.

options.text: The most capable tier, because this is a one-off, high-stakes reasoning task where quality outweighs speed and efficiency.
options.why: When errors are expensive, the task is complex and volume is one, the trade-off tips decisively towards the most capable model.

explanation: Align the model with what matters: here quality dominates because the task is complex, singular and costly to get wrong, while speed and volume are irrelevant. That is the profile for the most capable tier, with human verification of the result still required.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: A project manager drafts daily stand-up notes, weekly status updates and the occasional risk summary. The tasks are moderately complex, she wants good quality without waiting long, and she prefers not to switch models for every request. Which choice fits her everyday workload?

options.text: The most capable tier for everything, so nothing is ever under-served.
options.why: Using the heaviest tier for routine notes trades away speed and usage for quality gains the tasks do not need.

options.text: The fastest tier for everything, since notes and updates are short.
options.why: Short output is not the same as simple work; risk summaries and status updates need judgment that the lightest tier is least suited to.

options.text: The balanced tier as her default, stepping up to the most capable tier only for an unusually complex analysis.
options.why: The balanced tier is designed for the vast majority of everyday writing and analysis, and reserving the top tier for exceptions matches her preference not to switch constantly.

options.text: Turning on maximum effort and extended thinking on the fastest tier for every request, so she gets the fastest model's speed with deeper reasoning when a note needs it.
options.why: Maximising effort on every routine note adds latency she does not want, and it still does not give the reasoning depth of a higher tier when she needs it.

explanation: For a mixed, moderately complex everyday workload the balanced tier is the right default: it delivers good quality quickly for most tasks, and the occasional hard problem can be escalated to the most capable tier rather than paying for it on every request.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: A marketing operations team runs a three-step campaign process: (1) tag 10,000 social-media comments as positive, neutral or negative; (2) write 50 short campaign concept briefs; (3) produce one strategic positioning analysis for the CMO that weighs market data, brand risk and budget. Which two model assignments best balance quality, speed and cost across the process? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use the fastest tier for step 1, the sentiment tagging.
options.why: Tagging 10,000 short comments is simple, repetitive and high-volume, exactly where the fastest, most efficient tier fits.

options.text: Use the most capable tier for step 1, since the volume makes accuracy across many items critical.
options.why: Volume does not make a simple classification harder; the heaviest tier on 10,000 trivial items maximises time and usage for little gain.

options.text: Use the most capable tier for step 3, the CMO positioning analysis.
options.why: A single high-stakes analysis with several interacting constraints is the case where reasoning depth matters more than speed or cost.

options.text: Use the fastest tier for step 3, because it is a single document and will be quick either way.
options.why: The analysis is one item, but its difficulty and stakes are the highest in the process; the lightest tier is least suited to it.

options.text: Use one tier for all three steps so the outputs are stylistically consistent.
options.why: Consistency of style comes from instructions and examples, not from a single model tier; uniform assignment either overspends on step 1 or under-serves step 3.

explanation: Fit the model to each step, not to the process as a whole. High-volume simple work goes to the fastest tier, the balanced tier covers ordinary drafting, and the most capable tier is reserved for the one step where reasoning quality is decisive.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings

stem: An HR team is choosing the model for a policy question-and-answer assistant in a Project that has the employee handbook as knowledge. It will be used hundreds of times a day, mostly for simple lookups, and answers about entitlements must be correct. On a 40-question test set the results were: fastest tier 37 correct, balanced tier 39 correct, most capable tier 39 correct; the fastest tier answered noticeably quicker. Which choice best fits the requirements?

options.text: The balanced tier, because it matched the most capable tier on the test set at lower cost and latency, and the test set should be re-run whenever the handbook changes.
options.why: Choosing the least expensive tier that meets the measured quality bar, and keeping the measurement current, is how to align cost, speed and quality with evidence.

options.text: The most capable tier, because policy answers are important and it is the top of the range.
options.why: The test set shows it gives no accuracy gain over the balanced tier for this task, so its extra latency and usage on hundreds of daily queries buys nothing.

options.text: The fastest tier, because most questions are simple lookups and it is quickest at high volume.
options.why: Three wrong answers in forty is a 7.5% error rate on entitlement questions, which the stated correctness requirement rules out regardless of speed.

options.text: The fastest tier, with "be extremely careful and accurate" added to the Project instructions to close the gap.
options.why: An exhortation does not measurably change accuracy; the decision should rest on the test results, not on hoping an instruction fixes the shortfall.

explanation: The best model-fit decisions are evidence-based: test the candidates on a representative set, then pick the cheapest and fastest tier that meets the required quality, and re-test when the inputs change. Neither prestige of the top tier nor speed of the bottom tier overrides the measured requirement.
reference: Claude Help Center — Change the model, effort, and thinking settings; What are Projects

stem: An HR coordinator drafted a job advert with Claude yesterday. Today she opens a new chat and types "Write the second advert in the same tone as yesterday's." Claude replies that it has no record of a previous advert. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Repeat the request more emphatically, since Claude keeps every chat in the sidebar and just needs to be told clearly which conversation to look in.
options.why: A new chat does not automatically contain earlier conversations; insisting will not surface content that is not in context.

options.text: Switch to a larger model, which has a longer memory of past conversations.
options.why: Model tier does not govern what Claude remembers across chats; that depends on memory, Projects or chat search.

options.text: Paste yesterday's advert into the chat, or keep the tone guidance in a Project so every new chat can use it.
options.why: Each chat starts fresh unless context is carried over deliberately: by supplying it, by storing it in a Project, or by relying on memory or chat search where available.

options.text: Report a bug, because Claude should always remember everything from previous sessions.
options.why: This is expected behaviour, not a fault; conversations are separate unless a persistence feature bridges them.

explanation: Claude does not carry a conversation's content into a new chat by itself. To reuse earlier work, paste it, store it as Project knowledge or instructions, or use memory or chat search on plans that offer them.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context; What are Projects

stem: A product-launch chat has been running for three days and is now hundreds of messages long. Responses have slowed, and Claude has twice contradicted decisions made on day one. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the chat going but restate the day-one decisions in every new message.
options.why: Repeating decisions inflates an already overloaded conversation and does not address the degradation that comes with length.

options.text: Ask Claude to summarise the decisions, open questions and constraints so far, then start a new chat (or a Project) seeded with that summary.
options.why: A concise handoff summary preserves what matters, and a fresh chat restores responsiveness and reliability; a Project keeps the summary available for later chats too.

options.text: Switch to the most capable model in the same chat so it can hold the whole three-day history more reliably and pick out the day-one decisions on its own.
options.why: Changing the tier does not shrink the conversation or remove the noise in it; the long context is the problem, not the model.

options.text: Tell Claude to remember the day-one decisions more carefully from now on.
options.why: An instruction cannot make a very long context behave like a short one; the earlier decisions are buried among hundreds of turns.

explanation: Very long conversations get slower, cost more usage and become less reliable as early details are crowded out. The remedy is to summarise the state that matters and restart in a new chat or a Project, rather than pushing a degraded thread further.
reference: Claude Help Center — How do usage and length limits work; Usage limit best practices

stem: A consultant works with Claude across many separate chats and is tired of re-explaining her client, her preferred report structure and last month's conclusions. Which three approaches effectively carry context from one chat to another? (Choose three.)

options.text: Put the client background and report structure into a Project's instructions and knowledge, and work inside that Project.
options.why: Project knowledge and instructions persist across every chat in the Project, which is exactly what recurring context needs.

options.text: Choose a larger model, since bigger models retain more from previous chats.
options.why: Model size affects reasoning within a conversation, not what is carried between conversations.

options.text: Use Claude's memory, or ask it directly to remember her working preferences, on a plan where memory is enabled.
options.why: Memory saves context about role, preferences and ongoing work so later chats start with it, and users can view and edit what is stored.

options.text: Give each chat a descriptive title so Claude can find and reuse it automatically.
options.why: Titles help the user navigate; they do not put an earlier chat's content into a new one.

options.text: End each engagement chat by asking Claude for a short summary of conclusions, and paste that summary at the start of the next chat.
options.why: An explicit handoff summary is a reliable, plan-independent way to carry the state that matters into a fresh conversation.

options.text: Keep one enormous chat for every client and never start a new one.
options.why: A single unbounded chat degrades and eventually hits the length limit, which is the problem persistence features exist to avoid.

explanation: Context persists across chats only when something carries it: Project instructions and knowledge, the memory feature (where enabled), or a deliberate summary handed from one chat to the next. Model size, chat titles and never restarting do not achieve this.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects; Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context

stem: A consultant on a paid plan must answer questions over a 300-page set of client procedures for the next six weeks. When she attaches all the files to a chat, she is told the message exceeds the length limit; when she attaches a subset, answers miss content from the files she left out. Which approach best fits the constraints?

options.text: Split the files across several parallel chats and ask every question in each of them.
options.why: Asking the same question in several chats multiplies effort and usage, and no single chat can see relationships across the full set.

options.text: Add the procedures as knowledge in a Project and ask questions in new chats inside it, letting the Project retrieve the relevant parts of the knowledge for each question.
options.why: Projects can work with more knowledge than fits in one conversation by loading only the relevant content into context for each question, and the knowledge stays available for six weeks.

options.text: Turn on memory and paste the files in one at a time over several days so Claude memorises them.
options.why: Memory records working context and preferences, not verbatim documents; it is not a mechanism for storing 300 pages of procedures.

options.text: Ask Claude to summarise the 300 pages into one page and use only that summary for all future questions.
options.why: A one-page summary discards the detail that procedure questions depend on; it trades the length problem for an accuracy problem.

explanation: When the material is larger than a conversation can hold and will be used repeatedly, a Project is the right container: its knowledge persists across chats and, on paid plans, retrieval loads only the relevant portions into context when the knowledge exceeds what fits at once.
reference: Claude Help Center — How do usage and length limits work; Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) for projects

stem: An education coordinator has used one chat for four weeks to redesign a course. She uploaded six syllabus documents in week one. Claude's recent answers contradict those syllabi, and the chat has now hit the conversation length limit. She needs to keep working with both the syllabi and the decisions made so far. Which two actions should she take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Before leaving the chat, ask Claude for a concise summary of the decisions, open questions and constraints to date, and use it to seed a new chat.
options.why: The summary carries forward the state that matters without the four weeks of noise, and the new chat restores room to work.

options.text: Switch to the most capable model in the same chat so it can reach further back to the syllabi.
options.why: The chat is at its length limit; changing model does not add room or make the early uploads more visible.

options.text: Add the six syllabi as knowledge in a Project and continue the work in chats inside that Project.
options.why: Project knowledge stays available to every chat, so the syllabi no longer depend on being early in one overlong conversation.

options.text: Turn on memory so Claude stores the six syllabi word for word for future chats.
options.why: Memory captures preferences and working context, not verbatim documents; the syllabi need to be Project knowledge or re-supplied.

options.text: Stay in the same chat and ask Claude to re-read the syllabi carefully before each answer.
options.why: The conversation cannot accept more messages at the limit, and an instruction cannot fix content that has been crowded out of usable context.

explanation: When a long chat degrades and reaches its limit, restart from a distilled summary and move the reference material somewhere persistent. Projects hold documents across chats; a handoff summary holds decisions; neither model choice nor memory substitutes for them.
reference: Claude Help Center — How do usage and length limits work; What are Projects; Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context
